title: The Horizon Threshold in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reward-Free Exploration
claim: A hidden correct action sequence keeps the agent in the good state, while any deviation sends it to an absorbing sink.
layout: Single panel, layered state graph left-to-right, diagonal arrows to sink row
description: A black-and-white state-transition diagram on a white background, drawn as a trellis with two rows of circular nodes. The top row has nodes labeled s-star, joined by horizontal arrows labeled a_0-star, a_1-star and so on. These arrows show that taking the hidden correct action at each step keeps the agent in the good state. The bottom row has nodes labeled s_sink. Diagonal arrows from each top node to the next bottom node are labeled a not-equal a_h-star, so any wrong action drops the agent into the sink. A horizontal arrow labeled with calligraphic A (the full action set) joins the sink nodes, which shows that the sink absorbs every action. The rightmost nodes are cut off at the image edge. The eye goes first to the top row of s-star nodes and the labeled arrows.
caption: Hidden key for the lower bound: only $a_h^\star$ stays in $\starState$; otherwise transition to $\sinkState$.
abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning in the setting of reward-free exploration, where multiple agents jointly explore an unknown MDP in order to learn its dynamics (without observing rewards). We focus on a tabular finite-horizon MDP and adopt a phased learning framework. In each learning phase, multiple agents independently interact with the environment. More specifically, in each learning phase, each agent is assigned a policy, executes it, and observes the resulting trajectory. Our primary goal is to characterize the tradeoff between the number of learning phases and the number of agents, especially when the number of learning phases is small. Our results identify a regime change governed by the horizon $H$. When the number of learning phases equals $H$, we present a computationally efficient algorithm that uses only $\tilde{O}(S^6 H^6 A / Îµ^2)$ agents to obtain an $Îµ$ approximation of the dynamics (i.e., yields an $Îµ$-optimal policy for any reward function). We complement our algorithm with a lower bound showing that any algorithm restricted to $Ï< H$ phases requires at least $A^{H/Ï}$ agents to achieve constant accuracy. Thus, we show that having $Î(H)$ learning phases is both necessary and sufficient when restricting the number of agents to be polynomial.
